q: Does Mitiq's CDR (Clifford Data Regression) primitive reproduce the same or better mitigation quality as ZNE and PEC on the identical Fig 5 toy circuit at p=0.1, and how does its sample cost scale versus PEC's quasi-probability overhead?
basis: This replication verified ZNE and PEC quantitatively but only checked that CDR is present in the package. CDR is one of Mitiq's three headline primitives and its comparative accuracy/cost trade-off on the exact benchmark used for PEC (Fig 5) is unstated in the paper and untested here.
next_steps: Add work/rep_cdr.py using mitiq.cdr.execute_with_cdr on the same H;X;CNOT circuit and DensityMatrixSimulator executor at p=0.1. Sweep num_training_circuits in {10, 50, 200} and fit_function in {linear, exponential}. Report mean |err| over 10 seeds side-by-side with the existing PEC and ZNE numbers, plus wall-clock and total simulator calls, to yield a three-way cost/accuracy triangle.

q: Do ZNE and PEC deliver the same relative-error reduction when the executor is swapped from cirq.DensityMatrixSimulator to qiskit-aer's noisy density-matrix simulator with a matched depolarizing model, i.e. does the multi-backend claim hold quantitatively rather than just structurally?
basis: The paper advertises Cirq/Qiskit/pyQuil/Braket support (C5 in the claims table). This replication only exercised the Cirq path; the Qiskit path is a separate code route through mitiq's converters and could regress silently without affecting Cirq numbers.
next_steps: Install qiskit + qiskit-aer in a parallel venv. Rebuild the Fig 5 circuit in Qiskit, wrap a NoiseModel with per-gate depolarizing_error(0.1). Feed it through mitiq.pec.execute_with_pec and mitiq.zne.execute_with_zne. Assert that the resulting mean |err| matches the Cirq numbers to within Monte-Carlo variance.

q: How does Mitiq's ZNE performance compare against newer error-mitigation techniques not in the paper (virtual distillation, subspace expansion, symmetry verification) on the same 2-qubit RB benchmark used for C3?
basis: The Mitiq paper is from 2020 (arXiv 2009.04417). Since then, virtual distillation (Huggins 2021) and symmetry-based verification have become standard comparisons. Whether Mitiq's ZNE is still competitive on canonical benchmarks or whether the newer methods dominate at the same sampling cost is an open, actionable question.
next_steps: Extend work/rep_zne.py: for each of the 20 RB circuits, additionally compute (a) a two-copy virtual-distillation estimator implemented from scratch in Cirq, (b) a symmetry-verification post-selection using the Z-parity conservation of the RB Clifford group. Report mean |err|, sample count, and classical post-processing time for each method vs unmitigated and vs ZNE.

q: What is the actual hardware-runtime overhead (circuit-count multiplier, wall-clock, calibration frequency) of running Mitiq ZNE/PEC on a real IBM Quantum backend versus the simulator overhead measured here, and does that overhead change the effective accuracy/cost trade-off?
basis: C5 (hardware runs) was not exercised in this replication. The paper reports hardware plots (Fig 3) but does not tabulate wall-clock or shot-count overhead in a form that lets a user predict cost on IBM's current queue-based system.
next_steps: Using IBM Quantum's free-tier open-plan devices (e.g. ibm_brisbane or a Falcon backend if still available), run the Fig 5 circuit with and without ZNE (scale factors 1, 3, 5) at 8192 shots. Log job queue-time, circuit count, and calibration age. Compare per-mitigated-estimate wall-clock to the simulator baseline collected here.

q: Can a lightweight ML-in-the-loop layer (choose extrapolation order, folding fraction, or CDR training-set size per circuit) inside Mitiq's calibrator interface systematically outperform the paper's fixed defaults on a diverse circuit corpus?
basis: Mitiq exposes a calibrator API but the paper uses fixed defaults for extrapolation (Richardson) and folding (random local). Whether per-circuit adaptive parameter selection --- driven by a small classical model trained on circuit descriptors --- yields a real accuracy win is untested here and, more broadly, unresolved in the current mitigation literature.
next_steps: Build a corpus of ~200 random 2-4 qubit circuits with varying depth and 2-qubit-gate density. For each, evaluate ZNE with (scale_factors, extrap_method) in a small grid and record the best combo. Train a scikit-learn regressor mapping (num_qubits, depth, 2q_gate_fraction) to the best combo. On a held-out set, compare the adaptive-choice mean |err| against Mitiq's default. If it wins by more than 1.5x on average, propose upstreaming a mitiq.calibrator.LearnedSelector.
